name: Femi Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I process health insurance claims for a private health insurer, in a processing centre on the edge of town next to a carpet warehouse. Clinics send us bills for scans, physio, knee operations, and I check each treatment code against what the member's policy covers. If it matches, I approve it, and if not, I write to the member explaining why. I'm still slow on the codes, my team leader Mrs Okafor has a laminated cheat sheet she gave me which I keep under my keyboard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work, and the team is decent, we do a collection for anyone with a new baby. What wears me out is writing refusal letters to sick people, and the pay. I send two hundred a month to my mum since my dad passed, and Ruth, my fiancée, is a teaching assistant, so there's not much left. We've got maybe two and a half weeks' money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market sorted it out, the hype didn't pay, so the money went elsewhere. That's how it should work. At church I'd probably say we should be thankful for steady work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, I'd still be worried, but about money, not AI. My mum's rent went up and she's asked if I can send more. If the software does take some of the code-checking, they might not hire when people leave, which means more claims each for the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try to get quicker on the codes so I'm not on the slow list. I'd use the AI helper they've added for looking up codes, now that people in my team say it's fine. And I'd look for Saturday work to cover what my mum needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I'm not worried about robots, I'm worried about the end of each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of Saturday work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brother Joseph at church runs a funeral home, and he sometimes needs bearers and someone to help set up. It's twenty-five pounds a service, cash. It's respectful work and I don't mind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You send two hundred a month to your mother. Has Ruth said anything about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth says family comes first, she'd do the same. But it means the wedding keeps getting pushed back. We've been engaged two years and I'd like to marry before thirty.

say: The **market sorted it out**, because the hype didn't pay.
We should be **thankful** for steady work, and get on with it like before.
think: I'm worried about **money, not AI**, since my mum needs more each month.
If software takes some **code-checking**, leavers won't be replaced and we each get more claims.
do: Get **quicker on codes** so I'm off the slow list.
Use the **AI code lookup** now that my team says it's fine.
Find **Saturday work** to cover what my mum needs.
feel: **Anxious** about the end of each **month**, not about robots.
S0.quote: I'm not worried about robots, I'm worried about the end of each month.
fieldNote: He was **already anxious** because of money he sends his widowed mother.
He sees the plateau through a **free-market lens**: the hype didn't pay.
His wedding is **delayed** by family duty, which he accepts.

steps.text: Use the AI code lookup tool now that colleagues trust it
Work Saturdays as a bearer at Brother Joseph's funeral home
Learn the treatment codes well enough to leave the slow list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the next picture. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's business, firms will use what's cheaper and new jobs will come from it. I'd say people should get apprenticeships, not benefits. At work I'd tell the younger ones to learn the tools so they're useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, claims checking is the exact thing it describes, checking and answering. My job shrinks a lot, and I'm one of the slower ones, so I'm worried. But I also think some people will be kept to handle complaints and odd cases, and I'd want to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools every day now that it's clearly happening, and ask Mrs Okafor if I can move to the complaints team. I'd also ask Brother Joseph if he'd take me on more seriously at the funeral home, maybe as a trainee. And I'd tell my mum I might have to send less, which would be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can see things to do. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why complaints, rather than staying on claims?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because complaints are people who are angry or ill, and the AI can't really calm them down. My team leader Mrs Okafor says I'm good on the phone even if I'm slow on codes. It plays to what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would telling your mother be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Terrible. She'd say don't worry, she'd manage, and then she'd skip meals. I'd probably ask my sister to cover half, she's a dental nurse and earns a bit more.

say: That's **business**: firms use what's cheaper, and new jobs come from it.
think: Claims checking is **exactly what's described**, so my job shrinks a lot.

do: Use the **AI tools** daily and ask to move to the complaints team.
Ask the funeral home about a **trainee role**.
Ask **my sister** to cover half of what we send our mum.
feel: **Worried**, but seeing things to do helps.

fieldNote: He publicly backs **markets and apprenticeships** while privately fearing his own cut.
He moves towards **complaints**, where calming ill people matters.
Family duty to **his mother** is the hardest part of cutting back.

steps.text: Use the AI claims tools every working day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much faster one. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too much too quickly, even for someone who believes in markets. Businesses should be free, but not to break whole towns in a year. At church we'd be talking about how to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's finished, there's nothing hands-on in it. Even complaints go, because the AI will be better on the phone than me. I'd be out by 2028, with my mum relying on me and no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Brother Joseph and ask to work full time at the funeral home, because that's hands-on and people want a person there. It gives me till robots around 2031, and honestly I think people will want humans for funerals much longer. I'd move into Ruth's parents' spare room to stop paying rent and keep sending something to my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray a lot, and I'd try not to let my mum see how scared I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's that or my mum going hungry, yes. I'd swallow my pride. But I'd want it to come with work or training, not just money for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry quickly and simply, at church, no reception. Ruth's parents would be happier with us married if we're living under their roof. That's the one good thing in this picture.

Businesses shouldn't be free to **break whole towns** in a year.

Even **complaints** go, since AI will be better on the phone than me.

S2.quote: Businesses should be free, but not to break whole towns in a year.
fieldNote: The fast scenario **strains his free-market views**, without him dropping them.
He bets that people want **humans at funerals** long after robots arrive.
He'd accept state help only **with work attached**.

steps.text: Work full time at Brother Joseph's funeral home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a little slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, so there's no excuse for anyone not to prepare. I'd say the churches and families should help, and firms should offer apprenticeships. I'd say it to the men's group at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The claims job still goes, probably by 2031 or earlier. But five years lets me get the funeral training properly, a certificate in funeral service, and maybe marry Ruth before it all changes. I think I'd be okay, but my mum worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the insurer for two or three years and do the funeral certificate at weekends, with Brother Joseph paying part. Ruth and I would marry next year as planned and put the honeymoon money into savings instead. I'd keep sending my mum money but ask my sister to share it from now on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but with my feet on the ground. I know where I'm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come around 2034. Is a funeral home really safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it isn't, the paperwork and the bookings go first. But carrying the coffin and sitting with the family, I can't see people choosing a robot for that. I might be wrong, but I'd stake my working life on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be okay. Why still alarmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'll still lose the job that pays my bills, and the funeral home pays less. Okay isn't the same as comfortable. And my mum's getting older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it well. Businesses will adapt and new trades will open up. I'd tell the young lads at church to get a trade now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can do this properly. I'd stay in insurance, maybe get to the complaints team, marry, maybe start a family. Then move into the funeral home before 2036, when I'm about thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the complaints team and use the AI tools when everyone does. I'd work some Saturdays at the funeral home to keep my hand in. Ruth and I would marry next year and try to save a deposit, even a small one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frightened. It's far off, but I know it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the deposit plan on your wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a hundred a month once we're married and sharing one place. It'd take years. Ruth's parents might help, it's what families do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about how the government handles this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it to pay firms to take apprentices, not pay people to stay home. If my generation has ten years, we should spend them learning something with our hands. That's my view.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have my mum depending on me and nothing saved. What would help is paid apprenticeships, where a business is helped to take on someone like me. And some kind of bridge for my mum's rent if I'm between jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who depend on us. I'm twenty-seven with no kids, so on paper I'm fine, but my mum depends on my wage. Lots of young people are quietly holding up their parents.

headlineQuote: Lots of young people are quietly holding up their parents.
portrait: Femi is **twenty-seven** and checks treatment codes on claims for a private health insurer.
He sends **two hundred a month** to his widowed mother and keeps delaying his wedding to Ruth.
He believes in **markets and apprenticeships**, though the fast scenario tests that belief.
He uses AI **once colleagues trust it**, and is better on the phone than on codes.
His route out is a **funeral home** run by a man from his church.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with his mother depending on his wage and nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** with firms supported to take him on.
A **rent bridge** for his mother while he is between jobs.
